title: CTR mode and the nonce-reuse catastrophe
summary: Build CTR from raw AES, then break it exactly like a reused one-time pad when a nonce repeats.

steps.title: CTR: AES as a keystream generator
body: **CTR** (counter) mode never encrypts the message with AES at all. It encrypts a **counter block** (a nonce plus a block counter) to make keystream, and XORs the message with it:
keystream block i = AES(key, nonce || i)

So CTR is a stream cipher: no padding, ciphertext exactly as long as plaintext, any block can be decrypted on its own, and decryption is the same operation as encryption. Step through it below: watch `counterBlock` change in its last byte, and each keystream block get used for 16 message bytes.
The price: if the same **key and nonce** are ever used twice, the keystream repeats, and you are back to a reused one-time pad.

steps.prompt: Why does CTR mode need no padding?
options: The keystream is XORed byte by byte, so the last keystream block is simply cut short
CTR only accepts multiples of 16 bytes
The counter absorbs the extra bytes
steps.explain: Only the counter blocks go through AES, and they are always 16 bytes. The message is XORed with as much keystream as it needs.

steps.title: Build CTR from raw AES
prompt: Write `byte[] Ctr(byte[] key, byte[] nonce, byte[] data)` where `nonce` is 8 bytes. The counter block for block `i` (starting at 0) is the 8-byte nonce followed by `i` as an 8-byte **big-endian** number (`BinaryPrimitives.WriteUInt64BigEndian`). XOR `data` with the keystream; the last keystream block may be used only partly.
Because XOR undoes itself, the same function decrypts. The tests check the keystream against raw AES on the counter blocks you were told to build.
starter: byte[] Ctr(byte[] key, byte[] nonce, byte[] data)
solution: byte[] Ctr(byte[] key, byte[] nonce, byte[] data)
for (int start = 0, i = 0; start < data.Length; start += 16, i++)
for (int j = start; j < Math.Min(data.Length, start + 16); j++)
template: byte[] DojoBlock(int i) { var b = new byte[16]; dojoNonce.CopyTo(b, 0); b[15] = (byte)i; return dojoAes.EncryptEcb(b, System.Security.Cryptography.PaddingMode.None); }
var dojoZeros = Ctr(dojoKey, dojoNonce, new byte[40]);
Dojo.Eq("a partial last block uses the start of AES(nonce || 2)", Convert.ToHexStringLower(DojoBlock(2)[..8]), Convert.ToHexStringLower(dojoZeros[32..40]));
var dojoMsg = System.Text.Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes("no padding needed, any length works");
Dojo.Eq("ciphertext is as long as the message", dojoMsg.Length, dojoC.Length);
Dojo.Eq("Ctr twice gives the message back", dojoMsg, Ctr(dojoKey, dojoNonce, dojoC));
hints: Copy the nonce into bytes 0-7 of a 16-byte counter block, then write the counter into bytes 8-15 with `BinaryPrimitives.WriteUInt64BigEndian(counterBlock.AsSpan(8), (ulong)i)`.
XOR `data[j]` with `keystream[j - start]` for `j` from `start` to `Math.Min(data.Length, start + 16)`.

steps.title: One repeated nonce breaks everything
body: GCM, the mode you will use most, is CTR plus an authentication tag. So all of this applies to AES-GCM too.
Encrypt two messages with the same key **and the same nonce**: the keystream `K` is identical, and

That is module 1's reused one-time pad, exactly. Anyone who knows (or guesses) one message reads the other. With GCM it is even worse: the repeat also leaks the internal authentication key, letting an attacker **forge** valid tags for messages of their choice.
- a **counter** stored with the key, incremented for every message and never reset (best when you can keep state), or
- 12 **random** bytes per message, which is safe for up to about 2³² messages per key; beyond that, rotate the key.

steps.prompt: Two messages are sealed with AES-GCM under the same key and the **same nonce**. What does this print?
code: byte[] key = new byte[32], nonce = new byte[12];       // the bug: a fixed nonce
using var gcm = new AesGcm(key, tagSizeInBytes: 16);
byte[] p = Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes(text), c = new byte[p.Length], tag = new byte[16];
byte[] p1 = Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes("attack at dawn"), p2 = Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes("attack at dusk");
byte[] c1 = Seal("attack at dawn"), c2 = Seal("attack at dusk");
steps.explain: The ciphertexts XOR to exactly the plaintexts' XOR, and the 11 zero bytes show precisely where the two messages agree (`attack at d`). No key needed.

steps.prompt: Is each nonce strategy safe for AES-GCM with a long-lived key?
items: a 64-bit counter persisted with the key, never reset
12 random bytes from RandomNumberGenerator for each message
a constant nonce compiled into the app
the current Unix time in seconds
a counter kept in memory that restarts at 1 when the service restarts
a fixed nonce, but a brand-new random key for every single message
steps.explain: The rule is about the (key, nonce) pair: it must never repeat. Timestamps repeat within a second or across machines, and in-memory counters repeat after a restart. A fresh key per message makes any nonce unique for that key.

steps.prompt: Besides revealing `p1 ^ p2`, what extra damage does a repeated nonce do in AES-GCM specifically?
options: It leaks the authentication subkey, so the attacker can forge tags
It reveals the AES key directly
steps.explain: GCM's tag is computed with a subkey `H`. Two messages under one nonce give the attacker equations they can solve for `H`, and with `H` they can make tags for any ciphertext.

steps.title: Read a message you were never given the key for
prompt: An app sealed two 32-byte messages with AES-GCM and reused its nonce. You captured both ciphertexts (tags removed, hex in the starter) and you know the first message, because it was a transfer you made yourself.
starter: byte[] p1 = Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes("wire 5000 EUR to account 12-3456");
solution: byte[] p1 = Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes("wire 5000 EUR to account 12-3456");
hints: The keystream is the same for both, so `c1 ^ c2 = p1 ^ p2`.

steps.title: Fix the fixed nonce
prompt: This helper hands out the nonce for every AES-GCM encryption, and it always returns zeros. Fix `byte[] NextNonce()` so each call returns a fresh 12-byte nonce from a counter: 4 zero bytes, then the counter as an 8-byte **big-endian** number. The first call returns counter 1, so `000000000000000000000001`.
(In a real system the counter is persisted with the key so a restart never reuses a value. Here it lives in the `counter` variable.)
template: Dojo.Eq("1000 more nonces are all different", 1000, dojoMany.Distinct().Count());
Dojo.Check("every nonce is 12 bytes", dojoMany.All(n => n.Length == 24), "a nonce was not 12 bytes");
hints: Increment `counter` first, so the first nonce is 1.
